rv.q: The whole thing is a pleasing, tuneful, heart-filled ode to small towns and American dreams.

Well, Broadway finally got itself an all-American musical in 'Hands on a Hardbody.' The question is, will an all-American audience go for it? It's hard to picture hotel concierges, travel agents and group sales ladies pitching tourists a show about some working-class stiffs from East Texas clinging desperately to a cherry-red pickup truck in a m...
By the end of the show, you'll swear that truck can dance.
That makes this gently appealing show a welcome change of pace, even if its folksy simplicity makes it a commercial challenge.
This scrappy, sincere new musical brings a fresh, handmade feeling to Broadway, which mostly traffics in the machine tooled.
For all the worthy effort to valorize lives not usually depicted in musicals, this has the opposite effect: It makes them seem petty.

But if you go into the show wondering why a gifted creative team would want to adapt the 1997 documentary about poor Texans in an endurance dpouftu gps b sfe Ojttbo qjdlvq, zpv bsf mjlfmz up mfbwf xpoefsjoh uif tbnf uijoh.
Hardbody has too puny an engine to take anyone very far.
Rarely has so much goodwill been so squandered.
The resulting confusion of tone proves fatal.
With all that going for it, Hardbody holds up better than you might expect.
Unfortunately, the music – a mix of country, rock and bluegrass – falls short of inspiring.
As is, it’s a bit of a missed opportunity.
The show's biggest problem is that it doesn't know what it wants to be.

The tuner coarsens its self-effacing, quietly observant source with cheesy soap-opera backstories, forced Lifetime-movie subplotting, and self-righteous hot-button-issue pressing in an obviously manipulative attempt to stir our emotions.

cn.t: Critics find this blue-collar musical about a Texas endurance contest sincere and well-performed, but uneven. Praised for its daring subject matter and talented cast, it's faulted for tonal confusion and missed potential.

vs.sum: The Lena Horne Theatre offers good sightlines from most seats, with clear views even from the rear mezzanine. The sound quality is well-balanced across the theater. However, the seating is quite tight, especially for taller patrons, which affects comfort. The theater's ambiance is enhanced by its historic architecture and restored interior, providing a charming atmosphere.
